CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chest pain and referral for evaluation of esophagitis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a new patient referred from the ER with a history of chest pain that occurred in early October 2026. She reports the chest pain began randomly without a clear precipitant and lasted for four days. She describes the pain as sharp, located in the center of her chest behind her breastbone, and felt like she was having a heart attack. The pain was worse with eating. She also experienced difficulty swallowing during this time. After four days, she went to the emergency room where she underwent EKG and blood tests, all of which were normal. The chest pain and swallowing difficulty resolved approximately three days after her ER visit. She has been asymptomatic for the past three months since the initial episode. She notes that she was going through a stressful job transition around the time this occurred.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
No abdominal pain. Bowel movements are normal. No additional symptoms reported since the initial episode three months ago.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Uterine fibroids, anemia, cholecystectomy (several years ago).

MEDICATIONS
Not discussed.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
No known family history of GI problems.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient reports being in a stressful job transition around the time of her chest pain episode. She is trying to lose weight.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: Mild tenderness to light palpation in the upper abdominal quadrants bilaterally. Lower abdomen non-tender. Otherwise normal exam.

RESULTS
Prior ER workup included EKG and blood tests, which were normal. Cardiac etiology has been ruled out.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Patient with history of acute chest pain and dysphagia that occurred three months ago, now resolved and asymptomatic. Differential diagnosis includes GERD, dyspepsia, esophagitis, musculoskeletal etiologies, and anxiety. Suspected anxiety attack related to job transition with possible musculoskeletal contribution. Given that symptoms have resolved and patient has been asymptomatic for three months, esophagitis is likely already healed. Discussed upper endoscopy (EGD) versus conservative monitoring. Patient elected to self-monitor symptoms and will call the office if she experiences any additional episodes of pain or concerning symptoms. If recurrent symptoms develop, EGD can be performed at that time. Patient to follow up as needed for any other GI complaints.
